newsitem.title: USA: Fed faces tough time in deciding next rate move.
newsitem.headline: Fed faces tough time in deciding next rate move.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent

The Federal Reserve faces a difficult task this month in deciding whether to raise interest rates again amid signs economic growth is slowing but inflation risks are rising, central bank sources said.
"It's going to be a tough call," said one source, who declined to be identified.

The central bank raised short-term rates a quarter percentage point in March, the first increase in more than two years, in a bid to ward off inflation. Fed policy-makers next meet to set interest rates on May 20.

Fed sources said they expect some policy-makers to argue at the meeting that the central bank has already fallen behind in the fight against inflation and needs to raise rates further. But other policy-makers are likely to advise caution and contend no further action is needed now, they said.

Much will depend on the position taken by Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, whose influence has grown within the Fed over the last year as he successfully resisted pressure from anti-inflation hawks for steep interest rate increases.

In a speech in New York on Thursday, Greenspan said he expected economic growth to slow later this year and early next year, adding the central bank would need to act if that does not prove to be the case.
"Should the expected slowing in the growth of demand fail to materialise, we would need to address any emerging pressures in product and credit markets," Greenspan said.
Some analysts read that comment as a sign that the Fed will hold off from raising rates later this month. But others argued that the Greenspan was leaving his options open.

Fed sources said there have been scattered signs the economy was slowing from its rapid 5.6 percent growth rate posted in the first quarter, the fastest pace in more than nine years. Auto sales have slipped, factory orders have tumbled and job growth has moderated.
The signs of slower growth, however, are by no means definitive and the fundamentals underpinning the economy remain sound.
One Fed source likened the situation to last year, when after rapid growth earlier in the year, the economy slowed sharply in the fourth quarter.
But it quickly bounced back, as wage increases and a buoyant stock market fuelled a burst of consumer spending in the early months of 1997.

So far, though, the rapid growth has not pushed up inflation, which has stayed mostly steady. But the risks of higher inflation are there, especially with the jobless rate at 4.9 percent, its lowest in more than 23 years.
"The risks are clearly to the upside," one source said.
Echoing comments made in the past by Greenspan, Fed sources said inflation has been held down by a variety of special factors whose influence may be waning.

Earlier in the economic expansion, workers were anxious about losing their jobs and held off from pushing for big pay hikes. But wages have begun to rise as workers have become more confident, indicated by various surveys and the surge in spending in the first quarter.
Companies have managed to hold down labour costs by trimming their outlays on health care and other benefits. But that can only last so long.

The strong dollar also has helped contain inflation over the past year by keeping down import prices. But the dollar has tumbled in recent days against the Japanese yen, which could signal higher import prices and faster inflation ahead.
Despite all that, one Fed source said, it is hard to make a definitive case that inflation will rise later this year and into next -- making the May 20 decision that much more difficult.
